definition: Secession means the formal act of withdrawing from a political union, federation, or organization.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word secession. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know secession should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The mountain province threatened secession after the capital ignored its demands for a full decade.
Withdrawal is milder than secession: a member can quietly withdraw from a committee without any formal, public break.
Rebellion is stronger than secession: rebels take up arms to overthrow a government, while a seceding region formally votes to leave it.

A breakaway is a splitting-off to form something new — a breakaway league, a breakaway faction — and the word often names the offshoot itself. Secession is the formal act of withdrawing from a political union, usually by vote or declaration. Every secession produces a breakaway; breakaway names the offshoot, secession the declared break.

A split is any division or falling-out — bands split, parties split, alliances split — and the word says nothing about how it happened. Secession is one specific, procedural kind of break: a member formally withdraws from a union or federation by declared act. Splits can be mutual and messy; a secession is one side's formal departure.

An exit is the plain, neutral word for leaving any arrangement — a company's exit from a market, a country's exit from a treaty. Secession raises the stakes and the formality: a member declares its break from a political union, typically to rule itself afterward. Exits can be quiet; secessions redraw maps.

When the six wealthiest clubs announced their secession from the national league to form a rival competition, fans of the smaller teams felt betrayed.
The clubs did not simply quit playing — they formally withdrew from an organization they belonged to in order to run their own.
That organized, declared break is what secession names.

In 1905, the ranchers of the Sorell Islands grew tired of taxes set by a mainland assembly they could reach only by a three-day sail.
Rather than riot or petition, they organized a vote, and that autumn the islands declared their secession from the colonial federation in a document signed by every district.
The declaration was courteous, almost formal to a fault: it thanked the federation, listed the statutes being dissolved, and named the date the break would take effect.
Mainland newspapers were startled to find the islands governing themselves within a season.
Historians still cite the episode as proof that leaving a union can be a matter of paperwork and resolve rather than of arms.
